findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No haemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus, or large-territory infarct.

findings: Structurally normal heart. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: A normal interictal neurological examination without any limb sign; no event seen during the examination
action_criteria.label: Examine for positive functional signs and focal deficits
action_criteria.rationale: The examination documents that there is no focal deficit pointing to a lesion and no functional limb sign; for her events the diagnosis rests on the witnessed semiology (preserved awareness, crying, no postictal confusion), which a video-EEG recording confirms.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Habitual events recorded on video with no EEG change and a normal interictal record
action_criteria.label: Record both types of habitual event on video-EEG
action_criteria.rationale: Twenty-six years of drug-resistant events labelled posttraumatic epilepsy, with preserved awareness and crying: recording both the motor and the staring events without ictal change reaches the ILAE documented level and gives the strongest basis for withdrawing three drugs (AAN 2025). Without the recording, the positive signs and the semiology of witnessed events support the diagnosis at a lower ILAE level of certainty (LaFrance 2013).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Carbamazepine and phenytoin induce each other and diazepam and sertraline, diazepam needs a slow taper after decades, and sertraline with ibuprofen raises the bleeding risk
action_criteria.label: Review the antiseizure drugs and benzodiazepine before withdrawal
action_criteria.rationale: Three drugs started for misdiagnosed events are to be withdrawn: the enzyme-inducer interactions, benzodiazepine dependence and her sulfonamide allergy decide the order and pace of the taper.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Quantifies comorbid mood, anxiety and dissociation with performance-validity measures to plan treatment; it does not make the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment
action_criteria.rationale: A battery would quantify her depression, anxiety and dissociation for the treatment plan, but it does not make the diagnosis, which rests on the examination, and it is the most expensive item on this pathway.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on positive diagnosis and on physiotherapy and psychological therapy for FND; no step of this patient's work-up depends on it
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on FND diagnosis and treatment
action_criteria.rationale: A literature search is background reading, not a clinical step in this patient's pathway; no step of the work-up depends on it.

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat MRI, CT, lumbar puncture, EMG or nerve conduction studies, evoked potentials, PET).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Start or escalate antiseizure medication for the functional seizures, or stop it abruptly.
Give benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.
Give gadolinium contrast without a specific indication.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (functional seizures) based on the semiology of the two types of habitual event (preserved awareness, crying, no postictal confusion), confirmed where recorded by both event types on video-EEG without ictal change, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show how the features of the events support it, and give written information.
Refer for psychological therapy by a clinician experienced in FND (CBT-informed) and treat the comorbid depression.

Give the patient, family and ward a written plan for typical events: keep safe, do not restrain, wait for the event to end, and do not give emergency benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.

Taper and stop carbamazepine and phenytoin one at a time, then diazepam slowly over weeks, under neurological supervision, once the events are securely diagnosed as functional (ideally with a habitual event documented on video-EEG) and there is no evidence of epilepsy.

avoided_actions.rationale: No cardiac question: her events are motor episodes with crying and staring spells, not syncope, and the cardiovascular examination is normal.
Rhythm monitoring answers syncope; her events are recorded on video-EEG with a persisting normal background.
No new focal sign after a head injury 26 years ago; a CT answers no question about the events.
No fever, meningism or encephalopathy; lumbar puncture has no indication and invasive testing reinforces the search for an organic cause.
FDG-PET seeks a seizure focus for epilepsy surgery; her recorded events have no ictal correlate, so there is no focus to seek.
Strength is normal and an EMG after the injury was normal; nerve conduction and EMG answer no question.
Sensation is normal; somatosensory evoked potentials answer no question about her events.

accepted: Functional neurological disorder - psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES) with dissociative episodes, misdiagnosed as posttraumatic epilepsy for 26 years

differential.key_features: Habitual events recorded on video-EEG without ictal change; co-occurring epilepsy remains possible in about one in five patients with functional seizures. Both event types were captured during reduction of two antiseizure drugs, with no interictal discharges in 5 days.

Can mimic functional seizures with bizarre movements and an obscured scalp EEG, but are usually brief, stereotyped and often arise from sleep; her events last about a minute, occur awake with crying and preserved responsiveness, and the posterior rhythm persisted throughout.

key_clinical_evidence: Five habitual events of both types (motor events with crying and spitting, and staring spells) were recorded on 5-day video-EEG without ictal change, during reduction of carbamazepine and phenytoin.
Semiology by history and on video favours functional seizures: preserved awareness and recall, crying, about one minute duration, no postictal confusion.
Twenty-six years of no response to three antiseizure drugs is a common course of misdiagnosed functional seizures; the mean delay to diagnosis is about 7 years.
The interictal examination is normal; brief bitemporal theta in drowsiness is nonspecific and does not support epilepsy.
Carbamazepine, phenytoin and long-term diazepam are to be withdrawn one at a time, diazepam slowly over weeks.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A diagnostic label applied 26 years ago is re-examined on positive evidence; the recorded events without ictal change show the episodes are functional. A head injury is a common antecedent of functional seizures as well as of epilepsy.
red_herrings.data_point: Head injury at 22 with episodes from four months later, labelled posttraumatic epilepsy for 26 years
red_herrings.intended_effect: Accept the long-standing diagnosis and escalate or continue antiseizure treatment

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Brief bitemporal theta in drowsiness is a nonspecific finding and not an epileptiform discharge.
red_herrings.data_point: Intermittent bitemporal theta in drowsiness on video-EEG
red_herrings.intended_effect: Read the theta as supporting temporal lobe epilepsy

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A paternal uncle with childhood epilepsy does not make her events epileptic; the recorded events without ictal change do the opposite.
red_herrings.data_point: Paternal uncle with epilepsy diagnosed in childhood
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on an inherited epileptic cause

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Depression neither establishes nor refutes FND; it is a treatment target.
red_herrings.data_point: Major depressive disorder diagnosed at age 30, treated with sertraline and ten years of psychotherapy
red_herrings.intended_effect: Label the events psychiatric without positive evidence, or conclude that failed psychotherapy argues against a functional cause

findings.result: Strength 5/5 in all four limbs with consistent effort; no pronator drift, no give-way weakness.
No tremor or other involuntary movement at rest, on posture or in action.
Normal gait and tandem gait; Romberg negative.
Reflexes 2+ and symmetric, plantar responses flexor, no Hoffman sign; sensation and coordination normal.
No event occurred during the examination.

clinical_assessment.impression: No motor or sensory functional sign; neurological examination otherwise normal.

contraindications: Sulfonamide allergy (rash): avoid sulfonamide-structured drugs, including the antiseizure drug zonisamide.
Abrupt discontinuation of diazepam after long-term use: risk of withdrawal seizures and a withdrawal syndrome.
interactions: Carbamazepine with phenytoin: mutual enzyme induction; phenytoin lowers carbamazepine levels and carbamazepine raises or lowers phenytoin levels unpredictably. Changing one alters the level of the other, so dose changes are made one drug at a time with levels as needed.
Sertraline with phenytoin: sertraline can raise phenytoin levels (CYP2C9 and CYP2C19 inhibition); watch for phenytoin toxicity (nystagmus, ataxia, sedation).

Carbamazepine and phenytoin with sertraline and diazepam: both inducers lower sertraline and diazepam levels; as the inducers are withdrawn, sertraline and diazepam levels rise over 2 to 3 weeks, with more sedation and serotonergic adverse effects.
Carbamazepine with sertraline: both can cause hyponatremia (SIADH); the risk is additive.
Sertraline with ibuprofen: SSRI with an NSAID increases the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding.
general.proposed: Carbamazepine 400 mg twice daily; Phenytoin 100 mg three times daily; Diazepam 10 mg twice daily; Sertraline 100 mg once daily; Ibuprofen 400 mg as needed, up to three times daily
general.summary: Two enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs interact with each other and with diazepam and sertraline; long-term diazepam needs a slow taper; sertraline with ibuprofen raises bleeding risk; the sulfonamide allergy excludes zonisamide.
warnings: Diazepam after many years of use: physical dependence; reduce gradually over weeks to months.
Carbamazepine and phenytoin: abrupt withdrawal of an antiseizure drug can provoke rebound seizures; reduce gradually.
Concomitant CNS depressants (diazepam with antiseizure drugs): additive sedation and falls.

artifacts.impact: Moderate artifact during major motor events, but underlying cerebral activity clearly identifiable throughout all events due to persistent posterior dominant rhythm visible in posterior leads

background.posterior_dominant_rhythm: 10 Hz alpha rhythm, symmetric, reactive to eye opening
background.sleep_features: Normal sleep architecture with vertex waves, K-complexes, and sleep spindles. All sleep stages recorded. No interictal epileptiform discharges during sleep.

findings.frequency: Three events over 5 days; durations 55, 70 and 65 seconds
findings.morphology: During all three events, the EEG showed persistent normal waking alpha rhythm with superimposed muscle artifact. No ictal pattern, no rhythmic evolution, no post-ictal slowing. Video review shows events beginning with jerking of the trunk, progressing to bizarre bilateral limb movements, leg shaking, spitting, and crying. Patient pointed to her head stating it hurt. Eyes open during events. Patient responded to questions during events and had no post-event confusion.
findings.type: Clinical events 1, 3 and 4: trunk and limb jerking with crying

findings.location: No clinical lateralization; no EEG correlate
findings.morphology: During both events, normal waking EEG background persisted. No 3 Hz spike-and-wave or other generalized epileptiform pattern. No focal rhythmic activity. Video shows patient staring with eyes open, not responding to verbal commands, but with normal EEG. During the second event, when her name was called loudly, she briefly startled before resuming the unresponsive state.
Brief runs of 5-6 Hz rhythmic theta over both temporal regions, 2-4 seconds, in drowsiness only; no sharp component and no evolution.

eeg.impression: This is a NORMAL video-EEG. Five habitual events were recorded (three episodes of trunk and limb jerking with crying and spitting, 55 to 70 seconds, and two unresponsive staring episodes, 45 and 90 seconds) without ictal EEG change before, during or after the events; the posterior dominant rhythm persisted during the events. No interictal epileptiform discharges. No electrographic seizures. Brief bitemporal theta in drowsiness is a nonspecific finding.
eeg.limitations: None significant. Carbamazepine and phenytoin were reduced during monitoring (carbamazepine to 200 mg twice daily, phenytoin to 100 mg twice daily) to facilitate event capture; diazepam was continued at the usual dose. No epileptiform activity emerged during the reduction.

results.finding: Diagnosis of functional neurological disorder rests on positive clinical features such as the Hoover sign, tremor entrainment and functional seizure semiology, not on the exclusion of other disease; treatment combines explanation, physiotherapy and psychological therapy.
results.source: Espay AJ et al. JAMA Neurol 2018;75:1132-1141

results.finding: Motor signs such as the Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, drift without pronation and dragging gait have high specificity; sensory signs such as midline splitting have low specificity.
results.source: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190

results.finding: Defines levels of certainty for psychogenic nonepileptic seizures; the documented level requires a typical event recorded on video-EEG without ictal EEG change.
results.source: LaFrance WC Jr et al. Epilepsia 2013;54:2005-2018

results.finding: For functional seizures: assess for co-occurring epilepsy and psychiatric disorders, taper antiseizure medication without another indication, avoid benzodiazepines, and offer psychological therapy, which is possibly effective.
CBT added to standardised medical care did not reduce dissociative seizure frequency at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured CBT.
results.source: Goldstein LH et al. Lancet Psychiatry 2020;7:491-505

results.finding: Specialist physiotherapy for functional motor disorder was not superior to community neurological physiotherapy on physical function at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured it.
results.source: Nielsen G et al. Lancet Neurol 2024;23:675-686

results.finding: About 4% of patients diagnosed with conversion symptoms since 1970 later received another diagnosis.

functional neurological disorder diagnos.summary: Guideline and trial evidence supports a positive clinical diagnosis of functional neurological disorder, video-EEG confirmation of functional seizures, tapering of unneeded antiseizure drugs and benzodiazepines, and physiotherapy and psychological treatment whose trial effects on primary outcomes were modest.

metadata.condition_name: Functional neurological disorder - Psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES)
metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: onset after a head injury, a paternal uncle with epilepsy, nonspecific bitemporal theta on EEG and a 26-year label of posttraumatic epilepsy anchor on epilepsy; a prolonged video-EEG capturing both event types gives the documented level of certainty, and three drugs must then be withdrawn safely.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Severe, long-standing functional seizures misdiagnosed as drug-resistant epilepsy: the diagnosis rests on the event semiology, best confirmed by video-EEG, and management rests on a supervised taper of interacting antiseizure drugs and a benzodiazepine.
metadata.estimated_complexity: Diagnostic puzzle: 26-year misdiagnosis of posttraumatic epilepsy; event semiology makes the diagnosis, video-EEG documents it, and the drug withdrawal is supervised
red_herrings: Head injury at 22 preceding the onset of the episodes
Paternal uncle with epilepsy suggesting genetic predisposition
Bitemporal theta in drowsiness on video-EEG that could be misread as supporting temporal lobe epilepsy
26-year history of diagnosed posttraumatic epilepsy creating strong anchoring bias

Father with hypertension and type 2 diabetes
Paternal uncle with epilepsy diagnosed in childhood, well-controlled on medication
One brother (age 52) with no neurological conditions
Maternal grandmother with dementia (onset in her 80s)

medications.frequency: As needed, up to three times daily

Difficulty walking during recovery from head injury (age 22), evaluated with EMG which was normal at that time
Diagnosed with posttraumatic epilepsy at age 22, four months after the accident
Treated sequentially with phenytoin, carbamazepine, and diazepam without seizure reduction over 26 years

Ongoing financial strain due to unemployment and medication costs. Social isolation secondary to fear of episodes in public. Patient reports feeling that her life was derailed by the accident and the subsequent diagnosis of epilepsy.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mrs. Ramirez is a 48-year-old right-handed woman referred for inpatient evaluation of medically refractory seizures. Her seizure history dates back 26 years, beginning at age 22, approximately four months after she sustained a traumatic head injury in a bus-motorcycle collision. At the time of the accident, she did not lose consciousness but was hospitalized in the intensive care unit for several days. During her recovery, she experienced difficulty walking and underwent an electromyogram, which was reportedly normal. Four months later, she began experiencing paroxysmal behavioral and motor episodes occurring two to three times per week.

Her episodes are described as two distinct types. The first type consists of transient periods of unresponsiveness lasting several seconds to a few minutes, during which she appears to stare blankly and does not respond to verbal commands; her family refers to these as her 'absences.' The second type involves more dramatic motor manifestations: she describes a sensation of distress or agitation, followed by jerking movements of her trunk and extremities, bizarre posturing, leg shaking, spitting, and crying. These motor episodes typically last approximately one minute. After these events, she often points to her head saying it hurts but is able to converse with those around her and does not appear confused afterward. Her family reports that she seems aware during the motor episodes and can sometimes describe what happened immediately after.

She was diagnosed with posttraumatic epilepsy shortly after the episodes began and has been treated sequentially and in combination with phenytoin, carbamazepine, and diazepam. Despite adequate doses and good compliance, there has been no reduction in episode frequency over 26 years. She also underwent approximately ten years of psychotherapy and received antidepressant treatment, neither of which reduced the frequency of her episodes. She has been seen by multiple neurologists over the years, and the episodes have been attributed to refractory posttraumatic epilepsy. She is now referred for continuous video-EEG monitoring to characterize her episodes and guide further management. The patient is frustrated and frightened, expressing concern that her condition is worsening and that she will never be able to live a normal life. She is also concerned about the long-term effects of taking multiple antiepileptic drugs for decades.

neurological_exam.additional: Neurological examination is entirely normal between episodes. No focal deficits. No signs of lateralizing pathology.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin intact bilaterally. Rapid alternating movements normal in upper and lower extremities.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, reactive to light 3 mm to 2 mm bilaterally. Visual fields full to confrontation. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. Facial sensation intact bilaterally. Face symmetric at rest and with activation. Hearing intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline without atrophy or fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal gait with appropriate stride length and arm swing. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative. No ataxia.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Affect is anxious but cooperative. Speech is fluent without dysarthria or aphasia. Naming, repetition, and comprehension intact. Attention intact on digit span (6 forward, 4 backward). Memory 3/3 registration, 3/3 recall at 5 minutes. Clock drawing normal. Fund of knowledge appropriate for education level. No thought disorder. Patient appears distressed when discussing her episodes.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk and tone throughout. Upper extremities: strength 5/5 bilaterally in deltoids, biceps, triceps, wrist extensors/flexors, grip, and intrinsic hand muscles. No pronator drift. Lower extremities: strength 5/5 bilaterally in hip flexors, knee extensors/flexors, ankle dorsiflexors, ankle plantarflexors. No atrophy. No fasciculations. No involuntary movements at rest.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, and brachioradialis bilaterally. 2+ and symmetric at patellae and Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor (downgoing) bilaterally. No clonus. No Hoffman sign.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, temperature, proprioception, and vibration intact throughout all extremities. No dermatomal or peripheral nerve distribution sensory loss. Double simultaneous stimulation normal.
